Four questions we asked all semester

Question What it asks Where
Who can see it? Is the help a visible check, or hidden in the tax code? Week 1
Who deserves it? Whom does the public think has earned help? Week 12, Gilens
Who benefits? Who gains from things as they are? Week 3, Desmond
Who defends it? Once a program exists, who fights to keep it? Week 4, Pierson

Today’s question: what should change, and who has to give something up?

Howard: programs grew, but poverty didn’t fall

“There has been change, yes, but not much progress”

Christopher Howard, ch. 10, p. 197

  • U.S. poverty rate: 11.2% in 1974 (a recession year), 12.7% in 2004 (no recession)
  • Before taxes and benefits, U.S. income inequality is lower than in Belgium, France, or the U.K.
  • After taxes and benefits, it is higher. Howard: “the result of political decisions”

Howard 2007, ch. 10, pp. 193–94

Tax breaks for the better-off nearly match all aid to the poor

Biggest homeowner tax break, the mortgage interest deduction: taxpayers under $30,000 got 2% of it; over half went to those over $100,000 (mid-2000s)

Chart: Howard 2007, pp. 205–6 · mortgage deduction p. 205

Why so little progress? Howard sees four barriers

  1. States run many programs, and benefits vary by state

  2. The poor vote less, so officials hear them less

  3. Voters aren’t asking for redistribution (chart below)

  4. Tax breaks tilt toward the middle class and up

Chart: Howard 2007, table 10.1, p. 199 (General Social Survey) · pp. 197–203

Howard’s fix: aim the help at people who need it

Four changes he proposes:

  • Use tax credits, not deductions, and make them refundable, so people who owe no tax still get the money
  • Phase out tax breaks for high incomes
  • Set national minimum standards for programs the states run
  • Require employers to provide benefits, the way they must pay the minimum wage

His goal: programs that are “truly inclusive … (much like Social Security)”

Howard 2007, pp. 198, 207, 209

Campbell (Week 9): the programs’ own rules trap families

“keep a boot on their throats”

Andrea Campbell, on means-tested programs, ch. 4, p. 70

Three ways the rules trap people:

  • Aid is kept worse than the worst job (the old “less eligibility” rule, p. 57)
  • Earn more, lose benefits: a parent going from $10,000 to $40,000 keeps 45 cents of each added dollar, or as little as 20 (her 2014 example, p. 64)
  • Every state has different rules: “fifty different worlds” (ch. 5)

Campbell’s fix: the same protection for everyone

“Social insurance doesn’t work if it isn’t truly social”

Andrea Campbell, ch. 6, p. 117

  • Health care and long-term care for all; Germany’s care insurance costs a 1.95% payroll tax (pp. 115–18)
  • Paid leave and child care, so parents can work (pp. 121–23)
  • The same help in every state (pp. 124, 130)
  • Pay for it: U.S. taxes are 3rd-lowest of 34 OECD nations (p. 129)

Desmond: ending poverty costs less than unpaid taxes

Poverty gap: what it would take to lift everyone below the poverty line up to it, 2020. Desmond: “less than 1 percent of our GDP”

Chart: Desmond 2023, ch. 7, endnotes 12–14, 34 · ebook copy, no print pages

Desmond: more aid to the poor, less to the rich

His case that it works, Emergency Rental Assistance:

  • In the pandemic, Washington spent $46.5 billion helping renters
  • Eviction filings fell well below normal (chart)
  • Few cheered, and the program ended
  • Desmond: most aid today is “something like dialysis,” making poverty less deadly, not gone

Desmond 2023, ch. 7, endnotes 26, 28–31, 35 · ebook copy, no print pages

Desmond: give poor people more choices, so they can’t be exploited

“Choice is the antidote for exploitation.” (Desmond, ch. 8) What he proposes:

Choice in Desmond’s proposals
Work Raise the $7.25 federal minimum wage and end the $2.13 minimum for tipped workers. Let workers bargain for a whole industry at once
Housing Build more public housing. Help tenants buy their buildings as co-ops. Back small mortgages, as USDA’s rural loans already do
Banking End steep overdraft fees. Make payday lenders show what a loan will cost
Family Make birth control easy to get. Delaware did, and unintended pregnancies among low-income and uninsured women fell 24%, 2014–17
Your own life “Conducting an audit of our lives”: where we shop, invest, work, and study

Desmond 2023, ch. 8, endnotes 1, 6, 10–14, 18–20, 24, 27–30 · ebook copy, no print pages

Desmond: end the zoning rules that keep the poor out

  • Many well-off places ban apartments and small homes (“exclusionary zoning”)
  • His fix: lift those bans, and require new buildings to include affordable units
  • New Jersey’s courts made more than 340 towns build affordable housing
  • 1970: Nixon’s housing secretary, George Romney, proposed cutting federal money to towns that kept the poor out. Nixon killed it

Nixon cabinet meeting with George Romney, June 23, 1969 · Jack E. Kightlinger, White House · Nixon Library, NARA

Desmond 2023, ch. 9 and Epilogue (recommended), endnotes 9, 11 · ebook copy, no print pages

Three corners: stand with the author whose fix you’d back

  1. Stand up and go to the corner I point to for Howard, Campbell, or Desmond. Choose the fix, not the chapter you liked
  2. With the people in your corner, take 8 minutes to write two sentences:
    • What is wrong, as your author sees it
    • What should be done about it
  3. Pick one reporter. At 1:51 each reporter reads the two sentences aloud

What each author says is wrong, and how to fix it

What is wrong The fix
Howard Tax breaks go mostly to the middle class and up, states keep benefits uneven, and the poor have little political voice (pp. 197–206) Turn tax breaks into refundable credits, set national minimum standards, and make programs “truly inclusive” (pp. 198, 207, 209)
Campbell Families must stay poor to get care, and the help they get depends on their state (pp. 118, 124, 130) Cover everyone, as Germany does for long-term care; add paid leave and child care; pay with taxes that would still be low (pp. 116–18, 121–23, 129)
Desmond Poverty lasts because people who aren’t poor benefit from it (ch. 7) Make the rich pay their taxes, give the poor more choices, and end segregation (chs. 7–9)

1:51: each corner’s reporter reads its two sentences, about two minutes per corner

Round two: what would your fix need to work?

Stay in your corner. One minute to talk, then one answer per corner:

  1. What does another corner get right that yours misses?
  2. Desmond says people who aren’t poor benefit from poverty. Howard says voters aren’t asking for redistribution. Does your fix need a fight, or persuasion?
  3. Who has to give something up for your fix to work?

Poor People’s March, Washington, June 18, 1968 · Warren K. Leffler, U.S. News & World Report · Library of Congress

Last poll: does getting something make you defend it?

The case: the CSU’s contract for ChatGPT Edu, which you all have

  • The CSU paid OpenAI $17 million for the first 18 months (2025) and renewed for $13 million a year for three years (2026)
  • Who was in the room when it was signed? Has any group of users organized?
  • Compare AARP (Week 14): it claims 35 million members, but only one in six joined for its politics

Poll, same as Week 2: Does receiving something make you more likely to defend the decision that provided it? Hands up for yes.
